strengths: The motivating example clearly demonstrates why intervening on every controllable variable, or ignoring contextual information, can prevent recovery of the optimal policy. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b06/review-experiment-oa8d967e/call-26502668912e4efaa5ff9264e4402c46/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Combining causal policy-scope reduction with contextual Bayesian optimization offers a useful approach for continuous intervention domains, extending beyond the cited discrete mixed-scope methods.
Experiments report 110 seeds, 700 evaluations, and standard-error intervals. Including settings where baselines can attain the optimum usefully exposes the additional cost of scope search.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the approach combines existing POMPS characterization, HEBO, and standard UCB without a new scope-selection theorem or convergence analysis. The continuous-domain extension needs stronger technical or empirical evidence to establish a competitive contribution.

The justification for UCB selection is incomplete. Arm rewards change as their corresponding optimizers learn; stationarity at the optimum does not justify UCB during this learning process. Decreasing average regret over 700 iterations also cannot establish asymptotically sublinear regret or support the conclusion that the method always reaches the optimum.

The implementation does not establish support for general mixed policy scopes. Definition 3.1 allows different information sets for different actions and contexts downstream of earlier interventions, whereas Section 4 jointly optimizes all actions conditional on all scope contexts. Sequential execution and enforcement of each action's permitted information are unspecified.

Evaluation is confined to handcrafted synthetic environments with only one or two candidate POMPSes. Appendix C increases dimensionality primarily through redundant variables; it does not test scaling with the number of competing scopes. Scope-enumeration costs, optimization runtime, and realistic applications are not evaluated.

Missing ablations prevent attribution of improvements to the proposed selector. UCB should be compared with uniform allocation and acquisition-based selection using identical scopes and inner optimizers. The PSA experiments contain only one CoCa-BO scope, so their improvements cannot validate bandit selection. Baseline implementation details are also insufficient to establish matched comparisons.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing UCB settings, incomplete optimizer configurations, and no identifiable code link despite the release claim. Benchmark equations contain consequential inconsistencies: Appendix A.2 omits Cancer from the PSA equation although its optimality derivation requires that term, and Appendix C defines C4 using itself, contradicting the acyclic SCM. The stated regret sign also conflicts with the positive maximization-regret plots.
